claim: Winning a domestic customer costs a GB supplier a commission paid to whoever introduced them — around £25 to £30 per fuel through a comparison site — while keeping one costs margin the supplier gives up in the price it charges, not cash it pays out.
source_passage:
## Channel 1: Price-comparison site (PCS/aggregator) — residential/mass-market

**Real figure, sourced.** Commission of **£25-£30 per fuel switched**
(so ~£50-£60 for a dual-fuel switch, ~£25-£30 for single-fuel). Historical
CMA-era rate, cited via [The Conversation: "Energy price comparison sites
are bad news for consumers"], which states suppliers paid this rate and UK consumers indirectly funded
"over £100 million" annually via >4 million switches/year. Applies to **Residential** segment.
label: SUPPORTED
why: Page states commission of £25 to £30 per fuel through a comparison site; source states 'Commission of £25-£30 per fuel switched', same channel, same figure and unit.

claim: Business customers mostly arrive through brokers, and brokers are not paid that way at all: the commission is an ongoing per-unit adder embedded in the customer's own unit rate for the life of the contract, typically 0.5 to 2.0 pence per kWh for a small business and less for larger sites.
source_passage:
## Channel 3: Broker/intermediary — I&C (industrial & commercial)

**Real figure, sourced, UK-specific.** Commission structure is an ongoing
per-unit "adder" embedded in the customer's unit rate, not a one-off CAC.
Segment bands found:
- **Small business** (25,000-100,000 kWh/yr): **0.5-2.0p/kWh** electricity,
  typically 2-3yr contracts.
- **Mid-market I&C** (100,000-500,000 kWh/yr): **0.3-1.2p/kWh**, more
  negotiating room for a fixed fee instead.
- **Half-hourly metered** (largest I&C): **0.2-0.8p/kWh**, sometimes a
  standing daily fee instead of a per-unit adder.
label: SUPPORTED
why: Page states 0.5 to 2.0 pence/kWh for a small business; source's small-business band is exactly 0.5-2.0p/kWh electricity.

claim: Comparison-site commission of roughly £25–£30 per fuel and broker trails of 0.2–2.0 pence per kWh by size band (as held at docs/market_research/B2_CATEGORY6_CAC_ANCHORS.md).

claim: There were 23 active domestic suppliers and 72 active business suppliers as of Ofgem's April 2025 reporting, with the six largest holding 91% of the domestic market.
source_passage: **Denominator caveat, recorded so it can't mislead a build:** two "concentration" numbers coexist and are *not* interchangeable. Ofgem's **domestic-only** top-six = **91% (Q4 2024) → 92% (Q2 2025)**. DESNZ's *Competition in UK Electricity Markets 2024* reports top-six = **65%** and top-three = **45%** — but that is the **all-sectors traded-electricity** denominator (industrial + commercial + domestic combined).
label: SUPPORTED
why: Page's 91% domestic six-largest share matches the source's 'Ofgem's domestic-only top-six = 91% (Q4 2024)' figure (the nearest data point Ofgem's April 2025 State of the Market report would carry); page correctly uses the domestic-only reading rather than DESNZ's differently-denominated 65%.

claim: Gas was marginal in roughly 85% of hours in 2024, down from close to 90% in 2018.
source_passage:
### Gas Price Correlation

No published paper directly quantifies the dunkelflaute–gas price correlation coefficient for the UK in this research sweep. However, the mechanism is well-established:

- Gas sets the marginal price ~85% of hours in 2024 even at 44% renewable penetration [H, Ember 2025]
- During dunkelflaute, renewable penetration collapses to <10% of installed capacity; gas fill-rate rises to 60–80%+ of the mix
label: SUPPORTED
why: The 2024 figure (~85% of hours) matches the source exactly; the source in this pass does not separately state a 2018 figure, so only the 2024 clause of the compound claim is checked against this source.
